title: Architecture and flow diagram: how is the software or method structured?
summary: Boxes grouped into horizontal layers, joined by arrows that show which part feeds which. It teaches you to read a software or method diagram: what the layers are, what the arrows mean and what is left out.

media.alt: Layered architecture diagram with interface, core and data bands, nine boxes joined by solid data arrows and one dashed control arrow.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How is the software or method structured?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes. Three horizontal bands labelled interface, core and data. Boxes are components; solid arrows are data flow, one dashed arrow is control. The caption says arrows point downstream.
look_at: What are the layers, and what is in each one?
Which arrows are solid (data) and which dashed (control)?
Which box has the most incoming arrows (the hub)?
Do all arrows follow one rule, or do some point up between layers?
read_the_figure.proves: It describes the intended structure: what components exist and how data moves between them. It does not show that the code works that way, nor timing, size or failure behaviour.
if_wrong: Arrows with two meanings (call and data) and no legend: the reader cannot tell dependency from flow.
Layers whose rule is unstated: is a down arrow 'calls' or 'sends data to'?
Boxes of equal size for components of very different size: size suggests importance.

terms.meaning: A group of components at the same level of abstraction; the labelled bands.
A box: a module, service or data store with one role.
Solid arrow: data moves from the source box to the target box.
Dashed arrow: one component tells another what to do or when, without sending the main data.
A component with many connections; a single point of coupling or failure.

remember: Read the legend first: solid, dashed, arrow direction.
Layers group by role: interface (people), core (logic), data (storage).
Count in- and out-arrows: they show coupling.
A diagram is a claim about structure, not a test.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position in a layer encodes the role (vertical) and left-to-right groups related boxes; box colour repeats the layer colour (blue, teal, amber), so the layer is visible even without the band label. Line style encodes the relation type: solid for data, dashed for control. The bold box (model) is the focal component. A caption at the bottom is the legend.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A system is too large to describe in a paragraph but too connected for a list. A node-link diagram with layers gives two answers at a glance: what the groups are and who talks to whom. Colour per layer lets the eye follow a path between layers, and the arrow style separates two kinds of relation that would otherwise tangle.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What are the layers and the main path? Interface (CLI / config, dashboard, report export), core (data loader, model, optimizer) and data (raw files, feature store, results DB). The main path is raw files to data loader to model to optimizer to results DB. Q2: Which box is the hub? The model has three incoming arrows (dashboard, data loader, feature store) and one outgoing (to the optimizer). Q3: What does the dashed arrow mean? It runs from CLI / config to dashboard: configuration controls the dashboard but no data goes along it. Note also that two data arrows run upward from the data layer, so layers here do not mean top-down calls.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Layers labelled: the three band labels turn a set of boxes into a structure. Without them the picture is a graph with no statement about roles; with them the reader knows what kind of change each box allows.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A diagram simplifies: only 9 of perhaps 90 modules appear, and there is no way to see what was removed. Arrows are ambiguous unless defined: in this render arrows leave the data layer upwards (raw files to data loader, feature store to model) and go down elsewhere, so 'arrows point downstream' means data direction, not a layer hierarchy. Equal box sizes imply equal importance. Layers suggest strict separation that the code may not honour. The diagram ages: it shows the design on the day it was drawn.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of modules with their dependencies is exact and searchable. A UML component or sequence diagram shows order of calls. An automatically generated import graph shows what the code really does. A C4 diagram set gives several zoom levels.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the technology of each box in small type, the owner or file path, and annotate every arrow with the data it carries.

steps.title: Counting edges: in-degree and out-degree
steps.note: Every edge adds one to one in-degree and one to one out-degree. Here model has d_in = 3, loader and optimizer 2, dashboard and results DB 1.

steps.title: Coupling as the average degree
steps.note: On average each box touches two arrows; a hub with 4 connections stands out against this.

worked.title: Finding the hub by counting arrows
worked.problem: The diagram has the 9 arrows: CLI to loader, dashboard to model, report to optimizer, CLI to dashboard (dashed), raw files to loader, feature store to model, optimizer to results DB, loader to model, model to optimizer. Which box has the most arrows touching it?

solution.text: Count arrows ending and starting at the model.

worked.answer: The model has 4 arrows, twice the average: a change to it affects the most other boxes.

analyze.q: The raw files arrow points up into the data loader. What rule makes this consistent with 'arrows point downstream'?
What important element is missing that you would ask for before using the diagram to plan changes?
analyze.hint: Names of interfaces, file paths, failure paths.

evaluate.q: Would you accept this diagram as documentation of the code?
evaluate.hint: How could you check it automatically?

create: Redraw with every arrow labelled by the data it carries and a distinct style for call versus data.
Draw the same system as a table of module, depends-on and depended-on-by.

checks.q: What do solid and dashed arrows mean here?
checks.answer: Solid is data flow, dashed is control.

checks.q: A system has 12 boxes and 18 arrows. Average degree?
A new box is added that connects to 6 others. What does the diagram suggest about risk?
checks.answer: It becomes a hub with a degree well above the average, so any change to it ripples widely; consider splitting its role.
